signalslink:block-handbooktext-blocksens:
The block sensor detects the presence of a block at a selected adjacent position and, based on its type or input signal, provides information about its state or slot occupancy at the output.
The currently supported blocks are:
Anvil - if there is a sufficiently hot ingot on the anvil for forging, the Output signal is 1. Otherwise, it sends signal 0.
Doors, gates, trapdoors - For doors and gates, you need to monitor the block at ground level on the hinge side. If the block is open, the Output signal is 1; if it is closed, the Output signal is 0.
A chest or any container in general, or any blocks that have inventory slots (e.g. a campfire, barrel, trough, etc.). The Output signal is determined by the input signal.
The input signal determines which slot is to be scanned.
Signals 1-14 specify slots 0-13. The output is information about the occupancy of the slot relative to the maximum stack capacity of the item in that slot, converted to a signal from 0-15.
Signal 15 specifies that the sensor should detect the total occupancy of all slots, e.g. the entire chest.
Any other block not listed above - If there is nothing in the monitored area (there is air), the Output signal is 0. If there is water, the output is 2-fresh water or 3-salt water. If there is any other block, the Output signal is 1.

Paper Conditions
Paper Conditions are relevant to the block sensor when monitoring containers or blocks with inventories in general. If you have set Paper Conditions, the behavior of the block sensor changes as follows: If you are monitoring a specific slot (input signal 1-14), the conditions are applied to the item in that slot and, if it matches the conditions, the signal set in the output instruction in the conditional block where the match was found is returned. If output is not specified, signal 15 is returned.
If you are monitoring the total inventory occupancy (input signal 15), the conditions are applied to all items in all monitored slots. As soon as an item matches the conditions, the signal set in the output instruction in the conditional block where the match was found is returned. If the output instruction is not specified in the conditions, the number of the first slot where a match was found is returned.
Tip: You can use this to find out the slot number. Place an item in the slot whose number you want to know. Leave the other slots empty, then monitor this block with a block sensor to which you apply the paper condition "*" and send signal 15 to its input. The output will then be the signal with the number of the slot containing the item.
If no item in the slots matches the Paper Conditions, signal 0 is returned.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-entitysen:
The Entity Sensor detects the presence of entities (players, livestock, wild animals, or monsters) in the marked area and can provide information on its outputs about their count, type, or status. The sensor requires charging with one or more Temporal Gears to operate. The consumption rate then depends on the size of the monitored area.
Inputs x, y, z determine the size of the monitored area in blocks.
On the Error output there is signal 1 if the sensor is discharged, otherwise 0.
Inputs Output 1 setting and Output 2 setting determine what information will be provided on outputs 1 and 2. You can thus obtain different information on each output, based on these input settings.
The options are:
1 - The output returns Count. The number of detected entities.
2 - The output returns Category. Bit flags of entity category 0–3: player, creature, animal, wild animal.
3 - The output returns Life state. All detected entities are: 1–dead, 2–alive, or 15–mixed.
4 - The output returns Sex. All detected entities are: 1–male, 2–female, or 15–mixed.
5 - The output returns Age. All detected entities are: 1–young, 2–adult, or 15–mixed.
6 - The output returns Species. All detected entities are: 1–player, 2–animal, 3–wild animal, 4–creature, or 15–mixed.
7 - The output returns Reproductive state. All detected entities are: 1–ready to mate, 2–pregnant, 3–lactating, or 15–mixed.
8 - The output returns Reproductive state flags. Bit flags 0–2: ready to mate, pregnant, lactating.
9 - The output returns Minimum generation. The minimum detected generation is: 0–15. Present entities without a generation specified are ignored.
10 - The output returns Maximum generation. The maximum detected generation is: 0–15. Present entities without a generation specified are ignored.
11 - The output returns Minimum weight. The minimum detected weight is: 1–starving, 2–low, 3–decent, 4–good. Present entities without a weight specified (not animals) are ignored.
12 - The output returns Maximum weight. The maximum detected weight is: 1–starving, 2–low, 3–decent, 4–good. Present entities without a weight specified (not animals) are ignored.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-managedch:
The Managed Chute enables automated transport of items between different blocks. It transports items in only one direction, which is marked on the chute by a white arrow.
Unlike a chute, the Managed Chute does not have its own inventory and transports items from the block on the source side directly to the block on the target side. This means that items are not stored in the chute, but are only transported through it.
The Managed Chute has three Signals connectors: Input, Source and Target.
• Input is used to control transport. If the signal at Input is 0, the chute is inactive and transports no items. A non-zero value at the input triggers the transport of items from the source to the target. The following input values are supported:
1 - Transport one item
2 - Transport 2 items
3 - Transport 4 items
4 - Transport 8 items
5 - Transport 16 items
6 - Transport 32 items
7 - Transport 64 items
15 - Transport continuously.
Input values 1-7 allow items to be transported in batches. If there are not enough items in the source block to transport the requested amount, the chute transports as many as possible and transports the rest when another input signal appears. If you want to transport a different amount, you can send different signal values from 1 to 7 to the input in succession and thus compose the required batch size.
An input value of 15 causes the chute to transport items from the source to the target continuously, regardless of how many items need to be transported. The chute continues transporting items as soon as they appear in the source, until the input signal is changed to another value.
Transport takes place if something is available for transport on the source side and there is space to store the items on the target side at the same time. If either of these conditions is not met, the chute attempts to transport the items, but if this is not possible, it remains inactive until the situation changes (for example, items appear in the source or space becomes available in the target).
• Source is relevant if the input block is an inventory block. In that case, the signal at Source determines which slot the items are taken from. Signal 1-14 selects slots 0-13. Signal 15 means that items are taken from the last slot.
Signal 0 means that items are taken from any slot. In this case, the chute searches all slots and takes items from the first non-empty slot. If the source block has no inventory, this input is ignored.
• Target is relevant if the output block is an inventory block or air. For an inventory, the signal at Target determines which slot the items are stored in. Signal 1-15 selects slots 0-14.
If the target block is air and there is ground beneath it, the following Target values are relevant: 1 - the chute attempts to place a block from the source on the ground, 2 - the chute attempts to place an item on the ground if it can be placed. Signal 2 can also place a bucket, including its contents; the bucket will not be emptied.
The paper condition target ground forces this attempt regardless of the Target signal. It first attempts to place a block or bucket, and then possibly create a pile of items.

If the source block is air, the chute collects floating items from a 3x3-block area, where the middle block of this cube is the block in front of the chute opening. It can also pick up a bucket standing directly in front of the opening and insert it into the target inventory, including its contents.

In addition to the above, the Managed Chute can also insert items of type Ingot, Iron bloom and Blister steel into an anvil if the anvil is placed on the target side of the chute. When inserting ingots into an anvil, the plate forging recipe is selected automatically. In the case of Iron bloom and Blister steel, slag refining is selected to turn them into ingots. This is very useful for automating forging with an automated hammer. Before inserting items into the anvil, however, you must ensure that the inserted items are heated to the temperature required for forging.

Transport Filtering
The Managed Chute allows you to set conditions for filtering the items to be transported. Conditions are set using Paper Conditions, whose use is explained on this page
signalslink:block-handbooktext-managedwa:
A Managed Chute embedded in a wall enables automated transport of items between various blocks. It allows transporting items through walls, which can be very useful for hidden transport systems or for moving items from a cellar or into a cellar without disturbing the cool cellar environment, important for long-term food storage.
It works on the same principle as the Managed Chute. You can therefore find the usage description on the page describing the Managed Chute.
signalslink:usageinfo-signalslink-text:
SignalsLink
Extends the Signals mod with additional components.

To monitor a block nearby, you can use the Block sensor.
If you need to monitor your livestock, the Entity sensor is perfect for this.
If you want to automate some tasks, the Managed chute is ideal. It can transport items between blocks similarly to a chute, but you control it with signals and it gives you much greater control over what is transported. Its variant, the Managed wall chute, allows items to be transported through walls, which can be very useful for hidden transport systems or for transporting items from or to a cellar without disturbing the cool cellar environment, which is important for long-term food preservation.

The Managed valve is used for transporting liquids. Connect it with a hose to another valve or to an intake in water; longer lines can be assembled using hose couplings.
signalslink:usageinfo-paperconditions-te:
Paper Conditions are a shared rule system for Managed Chutes, Managed Valves and sensors. Write the rules on parchment and insert it into a supported device.

Basic principle
One paragraph on parchment forms one block. Separate blocks with one or more blank lines. Lines beginning with # or // are comments and are ignored.
All conditions in one block must be true at the same time (AND). Blocks are processed from top to bottom, and the first valid block is executed: its conditions must be true and its action must be physically possible. If the source has nothing, the target is full, or the action changes nothing, the block falls through to the next one.

Devices and actions
• A Managed Chute transfers items. It supports the source, target, target ground, amount, ifEmpty directives and the do seal action.
• A Managed Valve transfers liquids from the distant end of the hose to its host block. It supports the target, amount, ifEmpty directives, the do seal action and output 0 to 15. It does not transfer lava and cools hot water in the target.
• Sensors do not transfer anything; their default action is signal output. They support output; a sensor also supports output . for the number of the corresponding slot.
A block without an explicit action performs the device's default action. A block with output or do seal replaces the transfer: it transfers nothing, only sets the output or seals the barrel.

Code and attribute conditions
Exact code: game:resin. An asterisk * replaces any number of characters, while a question mark ? replaces one character: game:log-placed-*, game:ingot-?. A regular expression begins with @, for example @^game:log-placed-(oak|maple)-.*$. The prefix ! negates the condition, for example !game:resin.
A valid attribute name checks whether it is true. Comparisons use >, >=, <, <=, =, ==: temperature>1100, stackSize>=16, durabilityRatio>=0.75. The available attributes also include temperature, durability, durabilityMax, freshHoursLeft and isSpoiling.
Buckets and other liquid containers provide isLiquidContainer, liquidContainerEmpty, liquidContainerFilled, liquidCode and liquidLitres. For example, a full ten-litre water bucket matches liquidContainerFilled, liquidCode=game:waterportion and liquidLitres=10.
For liquids, patterns for world blocks and internal liquid parts work, for example game:water-*, game:water-still-7, *weaktannin* or game:waterportion.

Inventory and quantity
The inventoryAny condition checks any slot in the selected inventory, for example inventoryAny game:resin. It also checks liquids in liquid slots.
The pattern quantity condition checks the total quantity in the inventory: game:resin 10 means exactly 10, game:resin 10+ means at least 10 and game:resin 10- means at most 10. For liquids, the quantity is in litres and may have up to two decimal places, for example game:water-* 50 or *weaktannin* 20+.

Scope and transfer
in source switches conditions to the source inventory and is the default. in target switches them to the target inventory. Quantity conditions then count the entire selected inventory. You can alternate them within one block.
source N applies only to a chute and specifies source slot 1 to 14. For the corresponding block, it takes precedence over the Source pin. target N specifies the target slot, numbered from one. target N ifEmpty requires an empty target slot; after it is filled, the block falls through to the next one. target ground on a chute pointing into the air ignores the Target pin and attempts to place the item on solid ground. amount N sets the size of one batch. Signal 1 to 7 controls the total quantity in the buffer, while signal 15 transfers continuously. For a chute, an item batch is atomic; a valve transfers up to the specified quantity of liquid according to the source, target and remaining buffer.

Output and sealing
output X sets the output pin to a value from 0 to 15. The pin holds the last value until another valid block overwrites it. If the pin already has value X, the block changes nothing and falls through to the next one; therefore, a reset output 0 can be placed before a filling block.
do seal seals the target barrel if it can be sealed. It usually belongs after filling blocks. A sealed barrel cannot be sealed again.

Examples
game:log-placed-*
target 3
Transfers wooden logs to slot 3.

game:water-*
target 2 ifEmpty
amount 50

in target
game:water-* 50+
do seal
First fills empty slot 2 with water. Once the slot is no longer empty, the first block falls through and the second seals the barrel.

game:water-*
in target
inventoryAny *tannin*
in source
amount 5
Transfers water only if the target already contains tannin.

Setting up conditions
Write the conditions on parchment. Do not sign the parchment so that you can edit the text again.
Transfer the conditions to a block that supports them by right-clicking that block with this parchment. The conditions are then stored in the block, and you can see them in the information window when you look at the block.
To remove the conditions from a block, hold an empty piece of parchment in your hand, crouch (shift key) and right-click the block with this empty parchment. This deletes the conditions from the block.
If you want to copy the conditions from a block onto empty parchment, right-click the block with empty parchment without crouching.
Finally, here is a tool for finding out what code a block or item has and which attributes are available for use in conditional expressions:
Hold the item you are interested in in your hand, hold the ctrl key and right-click with this item on a block that supports Paper Conditions. The item's code and its attributes available for Paper Conditions are stored in that block. You can now copy them onto empty parchment, as described above, and freely edit them here into condition blocks and use them to configure the block.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-hosevalve:
The Managed Valve transports liquids through a hose. It always draws the liquid from the distant end of the line to its host. It has one hose anchor and two Signals connectors: the Input controls pumping, and the Output can be controlled using Paper Conditions.

Valve states
• Attached — the valve is placed next to a block with a liquid inventory, such as a barrel, bucket, or campfire. When there is a signal at the Input, it pumps liquid from the distant end of the hose into this host.
• Stand — the valve has no suitable inventory on its mounting side. In this state, it does not transport liquid; as soon as you place a suitable host block next to it, it attaches and starts functioning as an attached valve.
• Spout — a valve placed on the ground. When there is a signal at the Input, it releases liquid from the distant end of the hose; the liquid is not stored in the world, it is only displayed as droplets that soak into the ground. Useful if you need to get rid of excess liquid.

Pump control
Input signals 1 to 7 add a batch of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, or 64 liters. Signal 15 pumps continuously. If two Managed Valves are active on one hose, they alternate pumping.
The valve does not transport lava and cools hot water at the destination to the ambient temperature. Paper Conditions can filter the transfer, change the batch size, seal the destination barrel, or set the Output to a value from 0 to 15.

signalslink:ingameerror-hose-same-block: A hose can't connect two anchors of the same block.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-hoseintak: The intake is a passive source of water or salt water. Place it in water and connect it with a hose to a Managed valve, which will pump the liquid from it. Longer lines can be extended using hose couplings.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-hosecoupl: A hose coupling connects two sections of hose and extends the line between Managed valves or intakes. One section of hose can be at most 10 blocks long.
signalslink:item-handbooktext-hose: A hose connects the hose anchors of Managed valves, hose couplings, and intakes. One section can be at most 10 blocks long; couplings allow the line to be extended over a greater distance.
signalslink:ingameerror-hose-too-long: The hose can be at most {0} blocks long.
